props.title: Live music on your calendar, every week.
props.lede: You know the moment on a quiet night when your tables start asking for the check. A musician on your floor, on the same night every week, can give them a reason to stay for one more round.

headingText.html: We'll bring the same solo or duo act to your hotel or restaurant on the same night each week. If they can't make it, we'll send a backup you've already approved, and you'll get one invoice a month.
It’s built for a hotel lobby bar, a restaurant bar, a cocktail lounge or a member club, on a night that’s already busy or the one you want to build.

rows.text: A Colorado act you've watched on video plays at your venue every week, so your regulars get to know them.
If your musician can't make it, we'll send an act you've already approved. If we can't fill the night, you aren't billed for it. This is part of the Backup Promise.

rows.term: A different act if the first one isn't right
rows.text: Just tell us, and we'll bring in another act from our roster.

rows.term: Extra nights when you want them
rows.text: We can add a holiday night, a bigger act for a special evening, or a seasonal act like the Christmas jazz trio or the mariachi band.
The act brings a small sound system and keeps the music low enough that your guests can still talk.
We bill on the 1st for that month's nights, due in 30 days, and we'll send a certificate of insurance naming your property.

props.title: Does music keep guests at the table longer?
props.lede: Researchers have tested music in real restaurants for forty years. What they agree on most is that music changes how long guests stay.

rows.text: about 80 minutes

props.caption: Average time at the table across 282 tables in a 2024 experiment at one Italian restaurant in Tel Aviv. The size of the check didn't change.

rows.text: Slower music kept guests at the table longer, both in the Tel Aviv experiment and in a 1986 study in an American restaurant. That helps most on a night when you have open tables.
The studies disagree here. In the 1986 study, slower music went with more drinks ordered. In Tel Aviv, the check stayed the same. Guests who stay longer spend more when they order another round.

When 32 studies of music in stores were pooled in 2006, the effect was real and modest, and it grew when people liked the music. A musician can watch your guests and change the next song, which a playlist can't do.

We haven't found a study that compares live and recorded music on what a bar takes in. In a 2019 concert study, the audience moved more at the live show than another audience did to the same album played back.

props.html: Signet's founder, Daniel Fox, researches how music changes what people do. Read the full research summary, with sources, or his research notes.

props.title: How to start a weekly music program

rows.text: Tell us your nights, your space and your guests. We'll suggest two or three acts, and you can watch their videos.

rows.term: Try it for up to four weeks
rows.text: You can start without a long commitment. If the act fits, those weeks count toward your first 12.

rows.term: Twelve weeks, then month to month
rows.text: The program runs for 12 weeks at the program price. After that it continues month to month, and either side can end it with 30 days' notice.

items.a: Most venues start with one night, like a weeknight in the lobby bar or restaurant, or a weekend brunch. You pick the day and the time.

items.q: How long does the musician play?
items.a: They play for three hours, in three 50-minute sets. We can keep recorded music going during the breaks if you'd like.

items.q: What do you need from us?
items.a: We'll need a corner about 6 by 4 feet, one outlet, a stool, and about 45 minutes to set up before the first set.

items.q: What if we need to cancel a night?
items.a: Tell us 14 or more days ahead and you aren't billed for it. With less notice, the night is still billed.

items.q: What happens on the patio when the weather turns?
items.a: The musician moves inside, or plays a shorter night if you'd rather.
Yes. You'll get one invoice on the 1st of each month, due in 30 days. The first month is paid before the first night. We can set up as a vendor and work from a purchase order.

items.q: Do we need a license for live music?
items.a: Yes, and it's the venue that holds it. Live music is covered by public performance licenses from ASCAP, BMI, SESAC and GMR, and many hotels already have them. A license for background music, or one that comes with a music service, may not cover a live musician, so it's worth checking with each of them before the first night.

items.q: Does the musician put out a tip jar?
items.a: The musician only puts one out if you'd like one.
We quote per night after a conversation, based on the act and the nights you want.
